title: Intermittent decode stalls — root cause scratchpad
content:
Summary:
We keep seeing short, high-amplitude p99 spikes (~300–600ms) on small request paths (few tokens) in production clusters serving medium load. Spikes are intermittent (roughly 1–2% of requests) and appear to cluster in bursts lasting 30–90s. Median latency unaffected. Hypothesis: CPU-side stalls in the request decode/tokenization stage caused by interactions between Python GC, epoll/batch recv behavior, and heavy string manipulation in the tokenizer/normalizer.

Why this is weird / motivation:
- Spikes occur on tiny requests where model inference time is negligible; point of failure is before model dispatch.
- Not stable under load: when traffic saturates GPUs, stalls less visible (probably masked by larger model latency).
- Repro on staging is flaky, only reliably reproducible when artificially generating short requests at 200–400 rps on single-core worker.

What we observed:
- p99 jump correlates with short-lived CPU timeouts on worker process (top shows single core pegged to 100% for ~50–150ms).
- py-spy / perf top during spike shows stacks dominated by Python frames: tokenizer.normalize_unicode, re.sub (regex), bytes.decode, PyUnicode_FromStringAndSize, and a surprising amount of _PyObject_GC_Alloc / obmalloc activity.
- Flamegraph shows wide GC/allocator frames immediately before return to normal execution.
- strace on worker around spike windows shows clusters of recvmsg calls; some recvmsg return more bytes than typical (2–8KB) even though requests are small — suggests socket-level coalescing then Python splitting.
- Disabling preparse/fastpath in request pipeline reduces but does not eliminate spikes.

Quick numbers (staging synthetic test):
- baseline small request p99: 120ms.
- during spike windows p99: 420ms.
- measured CPU busy time in spike: 80–140ms user time consumed inside Python tokenization + allocator.
- sampling of tracemalloc shows ~5–12MB allocation churn preceding GC pause.

Preliminary root-cause hypotheses (ranked):
1) GC pause due to allocation spike from concatenation/slicing/regex during tokenization/normalization. Multiple concurrent requests on a single interpreter force repeated allocations and a generational collection at inconvenient times.
2) Epoll/recv batching causes sudden delivery of multiple small requests to a worker in a tight loop; our Python path processes them sequentially and allocation patterns amplify GC pressure (i.e., event burst => allocation burst => GC).
3) Jemalloc arena contention or fragmentation causing slow malloc/free path visible as Python pauses.
4) C-extension boundary costs (pybind/rust->py) where we repeatedly create many short-lived Python strings; GIL acquisition timing and GC interplay cause preemption stalls.

Experiments run so far (commands / notes):
- Profiling: py-spy record -o spike.svg --native --pid <pid> during a spike window. Verified long stack in PyUnicode/regex/GC frames.
- Perf + userspace stacks: perf record -F 99 -p <pid> -g -- sleep 10; perf script | Flamegraph.pl produced similar allocation-heavy stacks.
- tracemalloc snapshot: took before/after windows; heap snapshots show lots of small string objects (size 64–512B) alive briefly.
- Disable tracemalloc in staging (some overhead there) — no effect on spike frequency.
- Toggle CPython GC thresholds (PYTHONMALLOC=malloc vs default) in local: setting lower generational thresholds (so GC runs earlier) reduced spike magnitude but increased baseline CPU by ~5%.
- jemalloc switch: run with system malloc vs jemalloc build; observed small change in tail (10–15ms) but not root.
- Tokenizer micro-optimizations: replaced Python-level unicode normalization with C-extension wrapper to ICU normalize for a micro-bench; median tokenization reduced from 0.85ms -> 0.12ms and spikes frequency dropped in synthetic test. This suggests normalization is a prime allocation hotspot.

Repro recipe (staging):
1) Start single-worker serving-runtime process pinned to one CPU.
2) Run load generator: 250 rps of minimal text requests ("hi") with 10 concurrent clients for 2 minutes.
3) Watch logs/monitor for p99 spikes; collect py-spy/perf during spike windows.

Intermediate conclusions:
- The spike is not purely a threadpool scheduling issue (we've reproduced with single-threaded worker).
- Tokenization + unicode normalization produces allocation churn that triggers generational GC cycles that show up as CPU stalls.
- Socket coalescing/epoll burst delivery amplifies the effect: tightly-packed small events cause a flurry of allocations in quick succession.

Actionable mitigations tested and results:
- Move heavy normalization to C (ICU) via lightweight C-extension: large win in microbench, reduced spike incidence in staging.
- Adjust Python GC thresholds to be more aggressive (collect earlier): reduces p99 magnitude but increases baseline CPU. Needs trade-off analysis.
- Add a small per-worker inbound queue tokenization throttle (batching size cap) to avoid sudden bursts from recv coalescing — prototype reduced burst magnitude at cost of a few ms latency on first request in a burst.
- Rework tokenizer to use memoryview slices and reuse buffers instead of ephemeral Python strings: promising in unit tests but non-trivial refactor.

Open questions / unknowns:
- Is jemalloc arena tuning under our containerized environment a contributor? Need to run production-like jemalloc configs and measure.
- Could subinterpreters (if we adopt) help by distributing GC across interpreters? Complexity high and not safe for immediate change.
- Are there other C-extension hotspots beyond normalization (regex backrefs, emoji handling)? Need a full alloc profile per module.

Immediate next steps (prioritized):
- (High) Land ICU-based normalization C-extension prototype behind feature flag for canary. Measure spike rate over 24h in canary cluster. (Owners: Chen + Liam)
- (Med) Add transient ingress burst debugger: lightweight counter of recvmsg sizes + per-second recv bursts emitted to logs/metrics to correlate spikes with socket coalescing. (Owner: Maya)
- (Med) Experiment with GC tunables in a canary config (three variants) and run 48h A/B for p50/p95/p99 + CPU overhead. (Owner: Anika)
- (Low) Investigate jemalloc config/arenas on our k8s nodes; run malloc profiling. (Owner: SRE)

Notes to self:
- When capturing py-spy, use --subprocesses to see worker children if any; spikes can be masked by eBPF/proc sampling if done incorrectly.
- Keep an eye on Kubernetes pod scheduling that might co-locate too many host-level epoll producers.

Appendix: useful commands
- py-spy live: py-spy record -o /tmp/spike.svg --native --pid <pid> -- duration 20
- perf capture: perf record -F 99 -p <pid> -g -- sleep 10; perf script | ./flamegraph.pl > out.svg
- tracemalloc snapshot: python -c 'import tracemalloc; tracemalloc.start(); ...' (see local test harness)

End of scratchpad.

If you have other ideas or want me to run a specific microbenchmark or canary build, ping in #eng-serving-runtime and assign ENG-11234.
